questions.question: Q: What is the key difference between moist heat and dry heat cooking methods?

points.text: Moist heat methods use water or steam (boiling, steaming, poaching, braising) and are gentler. Dry heat methods use fat, oil, or hot air (baking, roasting, grilling, frying) and create browning and crispness through the Maillard reaction.

questions.question: Q: Why is steaming considered the healthiest method for cooking vegetables?

points.text: Steaming preserves water-soluble vitamins (B and C) because the food does not come into contact with water, retains colour and texture, and requires no added fat.

questions.question: Q: What is the Maillard reaction and which cooking methods produce it?

points.text: The Maillard reaction is a chemical reaction between amino acids and sugars at high temperatures (above 140°C) that creates browning and complex flavours. It occurs in roasting, grilling, baking, and frying.

questions.question: Q: Describe the three types of frying and how they differ.

points.text: Shallow frying: small amount of oil in a pan, for foods like eggs and stir-fry. Deep frying: food fully submerged in hot oil (160–190°C), for chips and battered foods. Stir-frying: fast cooking in very little oil over very high heat, for Asian dishes.

questions.question: Q: At what temperature does water boil and simmer?

points.text: Boiling is at 100°C (large bubbles breaking the surface). Simmering is just below boiling at around 85–95°C (small, gentle bubbles rising slowly).

questions.question: Q: What temperature range is used for poaching and why?

points.text: Poaching uses liquid at 70–90°C, just below simmering. This gentle heat prevents delicate foods (eggs, fish, fruit) from breaking apart or overcooking.

questions.question: Q: What are the advantages and disadvantages of microwaving?

points.text: Advantages: very fast, energy-efficient, retains nutrients well (short cooking time, no water). Disadvantages: no browning or crispness, uneven heating, not suitable for all foods (pastry, batter).

questions.question: Q: Why is grilling considered a healthier cooking method for meat?

points.text: Grilling allows fat to drain away from the food as it cooks, reducing the overall fat content. It also requires no additional oil, unlike frying.

markScheme.exemplarAnswer: Steaming cooks food over boiling water in a covered pan, without the food touching the water. This is the healthiest method: water-soluble vitamins (B and C) are retained because there is no leaching into cooking water, no fat is added, and the food's natural flavour, colour, and texture are preserved. Steaming is ideal for vegetables, fish, and dumplings. However, steaming does not produce browning or crispness, as the temperature does not exceed 100°C and no Maillard reaction occurs. Grilling cooks food under or over direct heat. Fat drains away from the food as it cooks, reducing the overall fat content compared to frying, and no additional oil is needed. Grilling creates browning and flavour through the Maillard reaction and gives a charred, smoky taste. It is well-suited to meat, fish, and some vegetables. However, very high temperatures can produce potentially harmful compounds (heterocyclic amines) in charred meat, so grilling should be done carefully and not to excess. Deep frying submerges food in hot oil (160–190°C), cooking it quickly and creating a crisp, golden exterior through the Maillard reaction. However, deep frying significantly increases the fat and calorie content of food as oil is absorbed during cooking. It is the least healthy of the three methods and is associated with increased risk of heart disease and obesity if consumed frequently.
